ing: snipped in half, seeds shaken out
st: Toss the chicken with [[1 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[1 tsp]] cornstarch and the wine. Let it sit for 15 minutes.
Whisk the remaining [[2 tbsp]] soy sauce, vinegar, sugar, [[1 tsp]] cornstarch and water in a small bowl to make the sauce.
Heat the oil in a wok or large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chilies and peppercorns and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant, taking care not to burn them.
Add the chicken in one layer and stir-fry for 4 to 5 minutes until browned and cooked through.
Push the chicken aside, add the garlic, ginger and scallion whites, and stir for 30 seconds.
Pour in the sauce and toss for 1 minute until it turns glossy and coats the chicken.
Stir in the peanuts and serve right away with steamed rice. The whole chilies are for flavor, not for eating.
Bring a pot of water to a boil with [[1 tsp]] salt. Slide in the tofu cubes and simmer gently for 2 minutes. Drain gently; this firms the tofu.
Heat the oil in a wok or skillet over medium-high heat. Brown the pork for 4 minutes, breaking it up.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the bean paste and cook for 1 minute until the oil turns red.
Add the garlic, ginger and scallion whites. Stir for 30 seconds.
Pour in the broth and soy sauce and bring to a simmer. Slide in the tofu and push gently with the back of a spoon; avoid stirring hard.
Simmer 5 minutes, then stir the cornstarch mixture and add half to the pan. Cook until the sauce thickens and coats the tofu, adding more if needed.
Serve topped with scallion greens and [[1/2 tsp]] ground Sichuan pepper with plenty of steamed rice.
Pat the duck dry. Pour boiling water over the skin to tighten it, then pat dry again. Rub inside with the salt and five spice.
Whisk the maltose or honey with the hot water and vinegar. Brush the glaze all over the duck skin.
Set the duck on a rack over a tray and refrigerate, uncovered, for at least 10 hours so the skin dries out like paper. This is what makes it crisp.
Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Let the duck sit at room temperature for 30 minutes and poke a few small holes in the fat near the legs.
Roast the duck breast side up on the rack over a pan with water for 45 minutes. Flip and roast 30 more minutes.
Flip it breast side up again and roast 20 more minutes at 425°F (220°C) until the skin is deep mahogany and the thigh reaches 175°F (80°C).
Rest 15 minutes, then carve the crispy skin and meat into thin slices.
Warm the pancakes. Spread each with hoisin, add duck, scallion and cucumber, and roll up.

ing: just boiled, plus extra if needed
st: Heat the broth, stir in the gelatin until dissolved, and chill in a shallow dish for 2 hours until firm. Dice into tiny cubes.
Mix the dough: stir the flour and hot water together, then knead 5 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest 30 minutes.
Mix the pork with the ginger, scallions, soy sauce, sesame oil, wine, sugar, salt and pepper. Stir in one direction until sticky, then fold in the gelatin cubes. Chill.
Roll the dough into a log, cut into 24 pieces, and roll each into a thin 3-inch circle with slightly thinner edges.
Put a heaped tablespoon of filling in the center. Pleat the edge in a spiral and twist to seal tightly at the top.
Line a steamer with parchment or cabbage leaves. Place dumplings on it with space between.
Steam over boiling water for 10 minutes. The pork must reach 160°F (71°C).
Let cool 2 minutes. Eat carefully, as the soup inside is very hot. Serve with black vinegar and ginger.
Mix the flour and warm water, knead for 8 minutes into a smooth dough, cover, and rest for 30 minutes.
Toss the cabbage with [[1 tsp]] salt and let sit 10 minutes. Squeeze out all the water with your hands.
Mix the pork, cabbage, scallions, ginger, soy sauce, sesame oil, [[1/2 tsp]] salt and pepper. Stir in one direction until sticky.
Cut the dough into 32 pieces. Roll each into a 3-inch circle.
Put a spoonful of filling in each wrapper, fold in half, and pinch the edges tightly closed with a few small pleats.
Boil a large pot of water. Add dumplings in batches and stir gently once so they do not stick.
When they float, add a splash of cold water. Repeat twice, about 7 minutes total, until the pork inside is 160°F (71°C).
Drain and serve with rice vinegar for dipping.
Mix the hoisin, [[2 tbsp]] honey, soy sauce, five spice, garlic, wine, sugar and sesame oil in a bowl.
Save [[2 tbsp]] of the marinade. Pour the rest over the pork in a bag and marinate in the fridge for 4 hours or overnight.
Heat the oven to 475°F (245°C). Put the pork on a wire rack over a pan with [[1 cup]] water to prevent smoking.
Roast for 15 minutes, then flip and brush with the saved marinade.
Lower to 400°F (200°C). Roast 20 more minutes until the pork reaches 145°F (63°C) and the edges are charred.
Mix [[2 tbsp]] honey with [[1 tbsp]] hot water and brush on the pork. Broil for 2 minutes until sticky and glossy.
Rest for 10 minutes, then slice against the grain and serve over rice.
Toss the pork with the soy sauce, salt and egg. Then mix in [[1/2 cup]] cornstarch until each piece is coated.
Make the sauce: whisk the ketchup, vinegar, sugar and water in a small pot. Mix [[1 tbsp]] cornstarch with [[2 tbsp]] cold water, stir in, and simmer for 2 minutes until glossy.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to 350°F (175°C).
Fry the pork in two batches for 4 to 5 minutes until golden and cooked through. Drain.
Raise the heat to 375°F (190°C) and fry the pork again for 1 minute for extra crunch. Drain on a rack.
Stir-fry the pepper and onion in [[1 tbsp]] of hot oil for 2 minutes, then add the pineapple.
Pour in the sauce, add the pork, and toss quickly just until coated. Serve right away so it stays crispy.
Slice the meat thin (freezing for 30 minutes first helps) and arrange on a platter. Arrange the vegetables and tofu on a second platter.
Heat the broth in a pot with the chilies, peppercorns, ginger, garlic and scallions. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 15 minutes.
Mix soy sauce and sesame oil in small dishes for dipping, adding garlic or cilantro if you like.
Move the simmering pot to a tabletop burner and keep it at a gentle bubble.
Add the harder items first: cabbage, tofu and mushrooms. Simmer for 4 minutes.
Using chopsticks, swish the thin meat slices in the broth for 20 to 30 seconds until fully cooked with no pink.
Dip the cooked pieces in the sauce and eat. Keep adding things as you go.
At the end, add noodles to the broth and drink some of the rich soup.
Mix the sesame paste, [[2 tbsp]] soy sauce, vinegar, sugar, garlic, ground peppercorns and chili oil in a bowl.
Whisk in the chicken broth until a thin sauce forms. Divide among 4 serving bowls.
Heat the oil in a skillet over medium-high heat. Brown the pork for 5 minutes, then add [[1 tbsp]] soy sauce and the preserved greens. Cook until crisp at the edges.
Boil a pot of water. Cook the bok choy for 1 minute, scoop out, and drain.
Cook the noodles in the same water according to the package, usually 3 to 5 minutes. Drain.
Put the noodles in the bowls on top of the sauce and add the bok choy and pork.
Top with scallions and toss everything together before eating.
Toss the chicken with [[1 tbsp]] soy sauce and the cornstarch. Let it sit while you cook the noodles.
Boil the noodles for 2 to 3 minutes until just tender. Drain, rinse with cold water, and toss with the sesame oil.
Heat [[1 tbsp]] oil in a wok over high heat. Stir-fry the chicken for 4 minutes until cooked through to 165°F (74°C). Remove.
Add [[1 tbsp]] oil. Stir-fry the garlic, carrots and cabbage for 3 minutes.
Add the remaining [[1 tbsp]] oil and the noodles. Toss for 2 minutes, letting some edges crisp.
Mix the oyster sauce, [[2 tbsp]] soy sauce and pepper, then pour over the noodles.
Return the chicken, add the bean sprouts and scallions, and toss 1 minute. Serve right away.
Soak the dried mushrooms in hot water for 20 minutes, then slice, saving the soaking liquid.
Bring the broth, strained mushroom liquid, mushrooms, bamboo shoots and ginger to a boil in a pot. Simmer for 5 minutes.
Add the tofu, soy sauce and sugar and simmer for 2 minutes.
Stir the cornstarch mixture and pour in slowly while stirring. Simmer 1 minute until the soup thickens.
Turn the heat to low. Slowly pour in the beaten eggs in a thin stream while stirring gently in a circle so they form ribbons.
Off the heat, stir in the vinegar, white pepper and sesame oil. Taste and add more vinegar or pepper.
Serve hot topped with scallions.
Break up any clumps in the cold rice with your fingers so the grains are loose.
Beat the eggs with a pinch of the salt.
Heat [[1 tbsp]] oil in a wok over high heat. Pour in the eggs and stir for 30 seconds until just set, then remove to a plate.
Add [[2 tbsp]] oil and the scallion whites. Stir for 15 seconds.
Add the rice and spread it out. Stir-fry for 4 minutes, pressing, until hot and lightly toasted.
Add the peas, soy sauce, remaining salt and the white pepper. Toss for 2 minutes.
Return the eggs, break them into small pieces, and toss with the scallion greens and sesame oil. Serve hot.
Put the flour in a bowl. Stir in the boiling water with chopsticks until shaggy, then knead 5 minutes once cool enough to handle.
Cover the dough and rest it for 30 minutes.
Divide the dough into 4 balls. Roll one into a thin 8-inch circle.
Brush with sesame oil, sprinkle with some of the salt and scallions.
Roll up like a cigar, then coil into a snail shape. Tuck the end under and press flat. Repeat with the rest and rest 15 minutes.
Flatten each coil with a rolling pin into a pancake about 1/4 inch thick.
Heat [[1 tbsp]] oil in a skillet over medium heat. Fry one pancake 3 minutes per side until golden and crisp. Repeat with each pancake.
Scrunch the hot pancakes slightly to open the layers. Cut into wedges and serve.
Mix the flour, yeast and sugar. Add the warm water and oil and knead for 8 minutes into a smooth, soft dough.
Cover and let it rise in a warm place for 60 minutes until doubled.
Toss the cabbage with [[1/2 tsp]] salt, wait 10 minutes, then squeeze out the water.
Mix the pork, cabbage, ginger, scallions, soy sauce, sesame oil and [[1/2 tsp]] salt well.
Divide the dough into 12 pieces. Roll each into a 4-inch circle, thinner at the edge.
Add a heaped spoon of filling in the center and pleat the edge up to the top, pinching tightly closed.
Place each bun on a square of parchment in a steamer. Rest 20 minutes to puff.
Steam over boiling water for 15 minutes until the pork is 160°F (71°C). Do not lift the lid for the first 10 minutes.
Rinse the rice until the water runs mostly clear. Drain.
Put the rice, water and ginger in a big pot. Bring to a boil, then lower to a gentle simmer with the lid slightly open.
Cook for 60 to 75 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes, until the rice breaks down into a thick porridge. Add hot water if it gets too thick.
Mix the pork with [[1 tbsp]] soy sauce, a pinch of salt and pepper. Drop small pieces into the congee for the last 10 minutes.
Cook until the pork is fully done with no pink, 160°F (71°C). Add the salt.
Boil the eggs for 7 minutes, cool in cold water, and peel.
Ladle the congee into bowls. Top with a halved egg, scallions, the remaining soy sauce and a drop of sesame oil.

ing: or light corn syrup mixed with honey
or 1/4 tsp baking soda in 1/2 tsp water
beaten with 1 tbsp water, for brushing
st: Mix the syrup, alkaline water and oil in a bowl. Stir in the flour with a spatula until a soft dough forms. Wrap and rest 1 hour.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Soak the egg yolks in the wine for 10 minutes, then bake them for 5 minutes. Cool.
Divide the lotus paste into 12 balls. Press a half yolk into the center of each and seal.
Divide the dough into 12 pieces. Flatten each into a circle and wrap it around a filling ball with thin even coverage.
Dust a mooncake mold with flour, press a ball in, and tap out. Or shape by hand.
Place on a lined tray and bake 8 minutes until set but pale.
Brush lightly with the egg wash and bake 12 minutes more until deep golden.
Cool completely. For the best flavor and soft skin, store in an airtight container for 2 days before eating.
Mix [[2.5 cup]] flour with [[0.5 tsp]] salt, then stir in [[0.75 cup]] boiling water with chopsticks until shaggy. Knead on the counter for 5 minutes until smooth and soft.
Cover the dough with a damp towel and rest for 30 minutes so it relaxes and rolls out easily.
Divide into 4 balls. Roll one into a thin round about 10 inches wide, brush with sesame oil, sprinkle with salt and a quarter of the scallions.
Roll the round up like a cigar, then coil it into a snail shape and tuck the end underneath. Flatten gently with your palm and roll out to a 6 inch disc. Repeat with the other balls.
Heat [[1 tbsp]] neutral oil in a skillet over medium heat. Fry one pancake for 3 minutes per side until deep golden and crisp at the edges.
Crush the hot pancake between your hands to open the layers, then cut into wedges and serve right away with soy dipping sauce.
nt: Pan-fried in a little oil
Best swap: use lard or scallion oil instead of sesame oil for a more traditional flaky flavor; same amount.

st: Rinse the plums, hawthorn and licorice root under cold water, then soak them in [[8 cup]] water for 30 minutes.
Pour everything into a pot and bring to a boil over high heat, then lower to a gentle simmer.
Simmer for 25 minutes with the lid slightly open, until the liquid is deep red-brown and smells sour and smoky.
Add [[0.5 cup]] rock sugar and [[1 tbsp]] osmanthus. Stir until the sugar dissolves, then simmer 5 more minutes.
Strain through a fine sieve, pressing the fruit gently. Cool, then chill in the fridge for at least 2 hours.
Serve over ice. Taste and add a spoonful of sugar if too tart.
nt: Simmered as a decoction, then chilled
Best swap: no wumei, use dried unsweetened prunes plus 1 tablespoon lemon juice, though the smokiness will be missing.

st: Chop half the shrimp into small chunks and mash the other half to a paste with a knife. Mix with the bamboo shoots, pork fat, sesame oil, sugar, white pepper and [[0.5 tsp]] salt. Chill 20 minutes.
Whisk the wheat starch, tapioca starch and [[0.5 tsp]] salt in a bowl. Pour in the boiling water all at once and stir with chopsticks until shaggy.
Knead the dough on a counter dusted with starch until smooth and warm, about 2 minutes. Cover with a damp towel so it does not dry out.
Roll the dough into a log and cut into 20 pieces. Flatten each into a thin 3 inch round using the flat side of an oiled cleaver or a rolling pin.
Put a heaping spoonful of filling in the center of each wrapper. Fold in half and pleat one edge about 7 times, pressing the pleats against the flat edge to seal into a crescent.
Line a bamboo steamer with parchment, leaving gaps between dumplings. Bring water in the pot to a rolling boil.
Steam over high heat for 6 minutes until the wrappers turn clear and the shrimp shows pink through them and is firm.
Serve right away while the skins are soft, with soy sauce or chili oil.
nt: Steamed over boiling water
Best swap: a mix of 3/4 cup potato starch and 1/4 cup cornstarch replaces wheat starch, but the skin will be less translucent.

st: In a bowl, mix the pork, shrimp, mushrooms, scallions, soy sauce, wine, sesame oil, cornstarch and sugar. Stir in one direction for 2 minutes until sticky and paste-like.
Chill the filling for 15 minutes so it is easier to shape.
Hold a wrapper in your palm. Put a heaping tablespoon of filling in the center and cup your hand so the wrapper gathers up the sides, forming a little cup.
Squeeze gently, tap the base on the counter so it stands flat, and smooth the top with a wet spoon. Press a pinch of minced carrot on top.
Line a steamer with parchment and set the dumplings in with gaps between them. Bring water in the pot to a rolling boil.
Steam over high heat for 10 minutes. The pork must reach 160°F inside and the wrappers should look glossy.
Serve hot with chili oil or soy sauce.
nt: Steamed over boiling water
Best swap: replace the shrimp with an equal weight of extra ground pork, or use minced firm tofu for a lighter vegetarian filling.

st: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and warm water. Knead for 8 minutes until smooth and elastic, then cover and let rise until doubled, about 1 hour.
Mix the pork with the ginger, soy sauce, sesame oil and [[3 tbsp]] cold water, stirring one direction until the water is absorbed and the meat feels tacky.
Stir in two thirds of the scallions. Chill until you are ready to fill.
Divide the dough into 16 balls. Roll each into a 3.5 inch round, thicker at the center. Fill with a heaping tablespoon of pork and pleat shut, pinching the top.
Rest the buns on parchment for 15 minutes, until slightly puffy.
Heat the oil in a nonstick lidded skillet over medium. Place buns pleat side down, fry 2 minutes until golden.
Add [[0.5 cup]] water, cover and steam over medium-high for 8 minutes until the water is gone and the pork reaches 160°F.
Uncover, sprinkle with sesame seeds and the remaining scallions, and cook 1 minute more to crisp the bottoms.
nt: Pan-fried then steamed in the same pan
Best swap: store-bought pizza dough works in place of the yeast dough, roll it thin and use about 1 lb.

st: Rub the butter into the flour and powdered sugar until crumbly. Stir in the yolk and [[3 tbsp]] cold water to form a dough. Chill 30 minutes.
Dissolve the filling sugar in the hot water and let it cool completely. Heat the oven to 375°F.
Roll the dough 1/8 inch thick and press into 12 tart molds. Prick the bases lightly.
Whisk the eggs gently with the cooled sugar water, evaporated milk and vanilla. Strain through a sieve for a smooth filling.
Fill each shell almost to the top. Bake 20 minutes until the custard just sets and reaches 160°F. Cool in the molds 5 minutes before unmolding.
nt: Baked at 375°F
Best swap: use whole milk plus 1 tbsp more sugar if you have no evaporated milk, or store bought shortcrust shells.

st: Mix the pork, shrimp, half the scallions, ginger, [[1 tbsp]] soy sauce, the sesame oil, white pepper and salt. Stir in one direction for 1 minute until sticky.
Place [[1 tsp]] filling in the center of a wrapper. Wet the edges, fold into a triangle, press out the air, then pinch the two corners together.
Bring the stock to a simmer in a pot and keep it hot. In a second large pot, bring plenty of water to a rolling boil.
Boil the wontons in the water in batches for 4 to 5 minutes until they float and the pork reaches 160°F inside.
Add the bok choy to the stock and simmer for 2 minutes until just tender.
Move the wontons to bowls with a slotted spoon, ladle the hot stock over, and top with the remaining scallions.
nt: Boiled dumplings in simmered broth
Best swap: finely chopped shiitake and firm tofu replace the pork and shrimp for a vegetarian filling.

st: Whisk the flours with the water and a pinch of salt until a smooth, thin batter forms with no lumps. It should pour like heavy cream.
Heat a large nonstick skillet over medium heat and wipe it with a little oil. Pour in half the batter and swirl quickly to a thin, even circle.
Cook about 1 minute until the top looks dry, then crack one egg onto the crepe and spread it with the back of a spoon. Cook the egg until fully set, with no runny parts, about 1 minute.
Sprinkle half the scallions, cilantro and sesame seeds on top, then flip the crepe carefully with a wide spatula.
Brush the cooked side with half the hoisin and chili crisp, lay two crackers in the center, and fold the edges over them like an envelope.
Slide onto a board, cut in half if you like, and repeat with the remaining batter. Eat hot while the cracker is still crunchy.
nt: Pan-cooked thin crepe on a hot griddle
Best swap: if you have no mung bean flour, use all-purpose flour only (increase to 0.75 cup total); crushed tortilla chips replace the fried cracker.

st: Heat [[2 tbsp]] oil in a wok on medium-low. Fry the shallots 10 minutes, stirring, until deep golden and crisp. Scoop out half.
Raise heat to medium-high, add the pork and fry for 8 minutes until lightly browned and fat renders.
Add [[0.33 cup]] soy sauce, [[0.25 cup]] rice wine, [[2 tbsp]] sugar, the star anise and [[1 tsp]] five spice. Stir 2 minutes.
Add [[3 cups]] water and the reserved shallots. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and cover.
Simmer 75 minutes, stirring now and then, until the pork is very tender and the sauce is thick and glossy.
Add the eggs for the last 20 minutes so they soak up the color.
Spoon over hot rice with some sauce, with a halved egg and pickled radish.
nt: Fried shallots, then slow braised
Best swap: dry sherry for Shaoxing wine 1:1; make it in a slow cooker on low for 6 hours.

st: Whisk the flour, cornstarch, salt and water until completely smooth. Rest the batter for 10 minutes so it thins out and cooks tender.
Stir the soy sauce, sugar and sesame oil together in a small bowl for the sauce. Beat the eggs with the scallions in another bowl.
Heat a 10 inch nonstick pan over medium-low heat and brush with a little oil. Pour in a third of the batter and tilt the pan so it spreads very thin.
Cook for about 1 minute until the edges lift and the top looks dry. Pour a third of the egg over the crepe and spread it evenly.
Cook until the egg is fully set with no runny spots, about 1 minute. Flip once and cook 20 seconds more. Brush with the sauce.
Roll up tightly, slice into 4 pieces and serve warm. Repeat with the rest of the batter and egg.
nt: Pan-fried thin crepe with an egg layer
Best swap: use [[0.5 cup]] rice flour for part of the flour to get a chewier crepe, and add cheese or ham inside for the modern version.

st: Stir the brown sugar into the hot water until fully dissolved, then let it cool for 15 minutes until warm.
Whisk the glutinous rice flour, coconut milk and [[2 tbsp]] oil into the sugar water until the batter is completely smooth with no lumps.
Grease an 8 inch round cake pan well with oil and line the bottom with parchment. Pour in the batter and tap the pan on the counter to settle it.
Press the red dates onto the top. Cover the pan tightly with foil so no water drips in.
Set the pan on a rack in a wok or large pot with boiling water below. Cover and steam on medium-high for 60 minutes, adding hot water as needed so the pot never boils dry.
The cake is done when it turns deep brown and a greased knife comes out clean. Sprinkle with the sesame seeds and cool completely, at least 1.5 hours, so it firms up.
Slice with an oiled knife. Eat as is, or pan fry slices in a little oil for 2 minutes per side until crisp outside and soft within.
nt: Steamed over boiling water for about an hour
Best swap: use 1 cup palm sugar or muscovado in place of dark brown sugar for a more traditional taste.

st: Stir the salt into the warm water. Mix with the flour in a bowl until shaggy, then knead for 10 minutes until smooth and firm.
Divide the dough into 8 pieces, roll each into a log, and coat with oil. Cover and rest for at least 45 minutes so the gluten relaxes.
Put the chili flakes, garlic, scallions, soy sauce and vinegar in a heatproof bowl. Heat the peanut oil until it shimmers and just starts to smoke, about 3 minutes.
Pour the hot oil over the chili mixture; it will sizzle loudly. Stir and keep warm.

Bring a big pot of water to a boil. Flatten one dough piece with a rolling pin to about a half inch, then pull it from both ends into a wide strip, slapping it on the counter. A pull of about 2 feet works.
Tear the strip lengthwise down the middle to make a thin center groove, then drop it into the boiling water. Repeat, cooking 2 pieces at a time.
Add the bok choy for the last 1 minute of cooking. Lift everything out with a strainer, drain well and pile into bowls.
Spoon the chili sauce over the noodles and toss before eating.
nt: Boiled hand-pulled noodles, hot oil poured over
Best swap: for no pulling, roll the dough flat and cut it into wide ribbons with a knife; use balsamic vinegar if you cannot find black vinegar.

st: Boil [[6 cups]] water with [[0.25 cup]] salt and [[2 tbsp]] sugar for 3 minutes until dissolved, then cool completely. Never pour hot brine into the jar.
Wash and dry the vegetables thoroughly, then air dry for 2 hours so the surface is not wet.
Add [[2 tbsp]] Shaoxing wine, the chilies, [[1 tbsp]] Sichuan peppercorns and ginger to the cooled brine in a clean ceramic crock or jar.
Add the vegetables, pressing them below the brine. Fill the jar no more than three quarters full.
Close the lid, add water to the groove if using a Sichuan crock, and leave at room temperature for 3 to 5 days.
Taste after day 3. When it is pleasantly sour and fragrant, refrigerate. Rinse and serve with congee or noodles; the brine can be reused.
nt: Brine-fermented, no cook; 3 to 5 days at room temperature
Best swap: use white wine for Shaoxing wine; for less heat, cut the dried chilies to 2.

st: Toss the shrimp with [[1 tbsp]] Shaoxing wine and a pinch of salt. Rub the cold rice between your hands to loosen the grains.
Heat [[1 tbsp]] oil in a wok over high heat. Stir fry the shrimp 2 minutes until pink and curled, then move to a plate.
Add [[1 tbsp]] oil and the beaten eggs. Stir quickly for 1 minute into small soft curds, then add the rice.
Toss the rice for 4 minutes, pressing out clumps, until every grain is hot and bouncing in the wok.
Add the ham and peas and stir fry 2 minutes until the peas are bright green.
Return the shrimp, add [[0.5 tsp]] white pepper and salt to taste, and toss 1 minute. Finish with scallions.
nt: Stir fried in a hot wok
Best swap: use diced Chinese char siu or cooked chicken for the ham, and sub 1 tbsp dry sherry for Shaoxing wine.

ing: pork belly or shoulder, in 2 inch chunks
flatbread dough balls, or pita for shortcut
st: Blanch the pork in boiling water for 3 minutes, drain and rinse off the scum.
Place the pork in a pot with the star anise, cinnamon, ginger, scallions, [[0.25 cup]] soy sauce, [[1 tbsp]] dark soy, [[2 tbsp]] wine, sugar and [[4 cup]] water.
Bring to a boil, cover and reduce to the lowest simmer. Cook for 90 minutes until the pork is very tender.
Remove the pork from the broth and chop it fine with a cleaver or large knife. Moisten with 3 tablespoons of the braising liquid.
Toast the flatbreads in a dry skillet over medium heat for 3 minutes per side until crisp outside and soft inside. Pita works too.
Split each bread like a pocket and stuff with the pork, green pepper and cilantro. Serve hot.
nt: Blanched then braised for 90 minutes
Best swap: use a slow cooker on low for 6 hours. Substitute pita for the traditional baked bing. Use shiitake and seitan for a vegetarian mix.

st: Soak the potato wedges in cold water for 5 minutes, then pat very dry. Whisk the soy sauce, oyster sauce, sugar, cornstarch mix and [[0.25 cup]] water in a bowl.
Heat the oil in a wok over medium-high heat to about 350°F. Fry the potatoes 5 minutes until golden. Remove.
Fry the eggplant 3 minutes until golden and soft. Remove, then fry the pepper 30 seconds and remove.
Pour off all but [[1 tbsp]] of oil. Add the garlic and stir 15 seconds until fragrant.
Return all vegetables to the wok, pour in the sauce and toss 1 to 2 minutes until it thickens and coats everything.
nt: Shallow-fried, then stir-fried
Best swap: use vegetarian mushroom sauce in place of the oyster sauce, and bake the vegetables at 425°F instead of frying.
